proxy_language: Proto-Kra-Dai / Proto-Tai (with Proto-Hmong-Mien and Proto-Austroasiatic as competing alternatives)
proxy_rationale: Zengpiyan (Guilin, Guangxi, c. 12,000-7,000 BP) is an archaeological culture with no linguistic record. Guangxi was historically Kra-Dai (Zhuang) territory, and Kra-Dai is the best-known language family of the region, but Kra-Dai is thought to have expanded from the coast or Lingnan only in the Neolithic-Bronze Age. Hmong-Mien and Austroasiatic are also plausible earlier occupants, and a lost isolate is possible. We therefore use reconstructed Proto-Tai (Pittayaporn 2009) and Proto-Kra-Dai (Ostapirat 2000) as a plain, internally consistent phonological model, flagged as a stand-in rather than an identification.
phonology: Proto-Tai (Pittayaporn 2009) consonants: stops *p *t *c *k *? and voiced *b *d *ɟ *g; implosives *ɓ *ɗ; fricatives *s *h *f *ɬ-type clusters in some reconstructions; nasals *m *n *ɲ *ŋ; liquids/glides *l *r *w *j. Vowels: *i *ɨ *u *e *ə *o *ɛ *a *ɔ with length contrast; diphthongs *ia *ɨa *ua. Three-to-four tone categories (A, B, C, D) arise from voicing and final-consonant splits. For naming, a simplified Zhuang-like phoneme set is used.
phonotactics: Mostly monosyllabic roots (CV(C)) with a sesquisyllabic tendency in Kra and Austroasiatic neighbors. Syllable shape (C)(C)V(V)(C). Initial clusters are limited (stop+l/r/w, e.g. kl, kr, kw, pl). Finals are restricted to *-p *-t *-k *-m *-n *-ŋ *-w *-j *-?; no voiced stops or fricatives in final position. Tones are not written in the scholarly reconstruction, so tone letters are omitted in names.
orthography: Plain Latin script modeled on Zhuang (1982 Latinized Zhuang) and Pittayaporn's Proto-Tai notation simplified for readability. Digraphs: ng, ny, kh, ph, th (aspirates), gv or kw for labialized velar, ae for the open front vowel. Vowels a e i o u plus ae/aw. No tone letters. Asterisks apply only to the labeled reconstructed forms in the roots list.
morphology: Isolating and analytic: little or no inflection, no case, no gender. Words are single morphemes or compounds. Limited derivational prefixes (a-, ta-, ma- nominal prefixes in Tai; classifier-like heads such as *ʔdaj / *kaj 'chicken, general animate'). Reduplication marks plurality or diminution in later stages but is not securely reconstructed. Numerals and classifiers precede or follow nouns depending on stage.
compounding: Head-initial: the head noun comes first, the modifier follows (Tai type: 'water river' pattern). Genitive/possession: possessed + possessor (e.g. 'house' + 'chief' = chief's house). 'X of Y' = X Y, with no linker. Agent/maker names use a head noun meaning 'person/master' + verb or noun, e.g. 'person fish' for fisher. Adjectives and demonstratives follow the noun. Names of places and objects are formed by head noun + modifier (Zhuang bya 'mountain', rungh 'cave').
noun_phrase_order: Noun + modifier (adjective, possessor, demonstrative, number-classifier order varies). Head-initial throughout.
sources: Pittayaporn, Pittayawat. The Phonology of Proto-Tai (PhD thesis, Cornell University), 2009
Ostapirat, Weera. Proto-Kra, Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 23(1), 2000
Li Fang-Kuei. A Handbook of Comparative Tai, University of Hawaii Press, 1977
Solnit, David. Eastern Kayah Li and comparative Tai-Kadai notes (reference); Zhuang standard grammar (Wei Qingwen)
Glottolog: Kra-Dai, Hmong-Mien and Austroasiatic family pages
Zhang Zengqi et al., Guilin Zengpiyan excavation reports (Chinese archaeological literature)
notes: No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word. Zengpiyan has no linguistic documentation; every form here is a model drawn from Proto-Tai and Zhuang, not a claim about the people's actual speech. Names should stay short, head-initial and monosyllable-based, with Zengpiyan's cave, shell and river setting reflected through roots like rung (cave), waj (shell) and nam (water).
